lines.en: It was lunchtime at Kumon-mi High, which meant Ami Arakawa was going to go sit in the classroom and wait for it to be over.
She didn’t need to. No one really hated her and her friends still existed. But she was going to anyway because it just never felt right being around them anymore.
And while her definition of “right” is clearly different from ours as evidenced by her place on the forced orgasm leaderboard, it’s still important that we respect her outlook and decisions.
Even when those decisions wind up pushing more people away.
But does she get that from her father? Or does he get it from her?
It’s an interesting question, I think. But one that won’t be answered today as there is a new elephant in the room.
And this one smells like earl grey.
: Oh, Arakawa Jr.
: Hm?
: How convenient. I just stepped out my office to come look for you and I’ve barely made it ten feet. Perhaps god is real after all?
: You’re looking for me? Why? Did I do something wrong?
: Wait — I’m not being transferred, am I? Because I know I’ve failed my last three quizzes, but I can promise you that there is a perfectly reasonable explanation for that.
: I am dumb.
: You’re not being transferred, Arakawa Jr. Though, this information will help me once again assert my superiority over Miss Imai, so thank you for that.
: Well, if I’m not being transferred and I’m not in trouble-
: Technically, I never said you’re not in trouble.
: Well, what did I do then?! You never come up to me and it’s scaring me based on what I’ve heard about you as a teacher!
: Just come with me to my office and we can talk more about that, okay? I promise I won’t inflict any harm upon you.
: I don’t know if I believe you after the whole janitor murder court case thing, since it wasn’t very clear if that was actually a real thing that happened or not.
: Well, if it was, it’s not as if we actually need them since all of you are perfectly capable of cleaning the school yourselves.
: You don’t have to remind me. I’m on cleaning duty today.
: I can get you out of it...for a price.
: Why are you blushing? Don’t blush. Stop that.
: I should have known the moment you asked me to come to your office. I just never realized you thought of me that way...but I guess it’s fine so long as it gets me out of cleaning duty.
: I swear, both you and your father are the same brand of infuriatingly suggestive. What a terrible combination the two of you make.
: You can do whatever you want to me in your office, but can we please not talk about him? It’s kind of a sore spot right now.
: I know. That’s specifically what I want to talk to you about.
: Oh!.......So you don’t want to tie me up then?
: No! And just joking about such things could cost me my job, so shut your delinquent mouth and just follow me to my office already!
: I doubt it could cost you your job, Miss Watabe. Far worse things have been both said and done in this school.
: What do you mean “done?” What do you know that I don’t?
: A lot, I imagine. But I’m not trying to get anybody in trouble, so- woah!
: Your office is so much nicer than my dad’s...I mean Sensei’s. I never know what to call him in school.
: You can call him your husband for all I care. Titles hardly make a difference now that no one can listen in on our conversation.
: Okay. Well, since you insist, I guess I’ll just have to call him my husband for the duration of this talk.
: I assumed you wouldn’t take that literally given your relationship with him is that of family, but I understand this one might be on me as I deluded myself into thinking you would know better.
: If it makes you happy, you can also refer to him as your husband, Ms. Watabe. Or shall I say — Mrs. Arakawa?
: You shall not. Ever again.
: Oh, come on. You know you’ve thought about it. Everybody has.
: That’s because everyone but me is an idiot.
: You don’t like him even a little? Really?
: I didn’t bring you here to solicit a date with your father-uncle-thing, Arakawa Jr. I’m more than capable of asking him out myself if I ever give up on the idea of happiness.
: Well, why did you ask me here then? Because you said it was about him. And normally, when someone says that to me, it’s because they want to sleep with him.
: I want to talk about both of you. As a...singular unit. And try to better understand the situation at home.
: You mean like a guidance counselor?
: That is technically part of my job here. Though, I imagine I’m supposed to be filling that role for my students rather than Imaikawa’s.
: Did you just combine Imani’s last name into mine? Does this mean I’m interracial now?
: No. It means you should take a seat before I need to open a secret drawer in my desk for something to strap you down with.
: Hey, I have one of those too!
: And I’m very happy for you, Arakawa Jr. But again, I am not here to allow you to keep deviating from the topic by tossing disgusting perversions at me.
: They’re hardly disgusting if you have a secret handcuff drawer.
: That’s not why they’re disgusting. But I imagine the age difference between us just doesn’t factor into your head at all seeing as your mother was the Girl Who Cannot Breathe.
: Oh.
: So you’re just saying it now. Directly to me.
: I understand that it’s a touchy subject, but I’m not here to debate the morality of her actions if that’s what you’re worried about.
: She was extremely talented regardless of the things that she did. And she passed that talent down to both your husband and you.
: Oh, please...I’m nothing compared to her. Winning your contest was a fluke.
: I wrote a million poems for that and Noriko’s was better than every single one. You only chose me because you wanted to learn more about my mom.
: That may have played some part in it. But I was under the impression you were unable to talk about her.
: Which isn’t even factoring in how Arakawa Sr. told me to stop poking my nose where it doesn’t belong and just stay out of it entirely.
: But you didn’t...and I’m supposed to believe you went through all of that effort just so you can tell me I’m talented? What do you really want, Ms. Watabe?
: Heh...that’s a good question.
: I spent so long trying to uncover the relationship between the three of you that hearing it straight from the horse’s mouth felt somewhat...anticlimactic when all was said and done.
: I’m not really sure what to do anymore.
: So am I the horse? Or is my dad the horse? Because I assume you talked to him and I assume he’s the one who put you up to this.
: Is this what you’re like when the charade drops? The two of you really do have so much in common, don’t you?
: There is no “charade.” I just try to limit the amount of people who know the specifics of my upbringing since all it does is garner pity and misunderstandings.
: Like I said — I’m not here to talk about morality. And I don’t need to read a dead woman’s non-existent autobiography to pity the girl she left behind.
: I’m here to remind you that you’re the only piece left of your mother. And that every second you spend away from your “father” is like her leaving all over again.
: He...told you to say that?
: Those are my words, not his. We both know how unwilling he is to put actual thought into any of what he says.
: I can tell you he’s hurting, though. That he’s sorry. And that he wants you to come home. Even if you’re a terror.
: Hah...
: Why did you run out anyway? Just trying to make him feel bad? Did you two get into a fight?
: Is this what you’re like when the charade drops? Nice?
: I have my moments, I suppose. And quite frankly, I think your family is rather disgusting.
: But Arakawa Sr. has taken up residence somewhere inside of my heart. And it’d feel wrong to just evict him when he’s already struggling so much.
: Do you pity him?
: Arakawa? Why? Because he was sleeping with your mother? Or because he’s a completely and utterly helpless excuse for a man?
: The mom thing. Like...there was another older woman who also found out about this recently and her reaction was way different than yours.
: You’re talking about that idol, aren’t you? Niki?
: Jesus. How close are you guys? Just how much did he tell you?
: He mentioned her leaving as well. But I knew the two of them were “together” before that.
: And yes, I do pity him. For both of the reasons I mentioned. And I pity you as well, regardless of how much you apparently want to avoid incurring such a feeling.
: It’s not even that I want to avoid it. It’s just...such a normal thing to me that it’s kind of annoying at this point.
: What I want more than anything is to just enjoy what’s left of my life with my dad. That’s all. And how am I supposed to enjoy anything with people reminding me of how sad we are all the time?
: You say that like you’re going to die soon.
: No, I say that knowing I can.
: Everything can end at any moment. A meteor could crash into this school right now and we’d all be burnt to a crisp. I could get an aneurysm. I could be murdered.
: Anything can happen. So when you spend every waking moment miserable, you’re taking away time from a very finite amount of happiness available.
: Life doesn’t just start over when you die. That’s it. You’re done. No more.
: And that’s exactly what happened to my mom. Before she ever had a chance to show everyone how amazing she was instead of just the people who met her.
: So tell me, Ms. Watabe — if she was so evil like you and all of your pretentious poetry friends think, why did everyone in her life love her so much?
: You overestimate the amount of “pretentious poetry friends” I have. Or that I’d want to discuss your mother’s works with them in general.
: They’re amazing though, aren’t they? You said it yourself. She was talented.
: Extremely. But there are certain truths in this world that are accepted inevitably, and your mother challenged nearly all of them. Which is precisely what she wanted to do, so-
: No, she didn’t want to do that. That’s just who she was.
: She was never afraid of being herself and I can’t even figure out who or what I’m supposed to be yet.
: So no, I didn’t inherit her talent. I inherited her scorn for a world that didn’t want her here, the infinite blame that accompanies it, and a pair of shoes I can’t ever fill.
: Me going home won’t make my dad happy again. It’ll just be more charades. A bandage on a wound that’s bleeding out.
: You know...you wouldn’t have to eat alone if you’d just show this side to other people.
: Stop pretending to care about me just because you care about him. Everyone always does that and I seriously hate it.
: But if I don’t care about you, I won’t get paid. That’s part of my job.
: Sure, but...it’s not everybody’s job and they all do it too, so...
: Do you think that Niki woman was only pretending to care about you too, then? Is that what you two got into a fight over?
: I don’t know...
: She just...
: Being around her causes him pain. And that causes me pain. So it’d be better if she just left.
: You think you two would be happier just ignoring everything then?
: Right...Yeah.
: Arakawa told me the same thing essentially. Just he’s not writing anything down like you are. So I’m sure you understand just how much he’s keeping inside.
: He will eventually...
: He just needs time.
: But until then, don’t you think it would help him having the one he loves the most by his side?
: Maybe...
: I just doubt if that person’s actually me sometimes.
: I know how you feel. Trust me.
: But I also know that Arakawa would not have asked me to try and bring you home if he did not literally need my help. And I want to help him because he helps me. So please-
: Go home. Make him happy. Or...try and fail, I suppose. Just be there for him.
: You know...you’d make a good mom, Miss Watabe.
: I go this far out of my way to help you and you say that? I’ve never felt so insulted in my life.
: It’s not an insult, I promise. If anything, someone like you might be nice to have around the house.
: A kind-hearted poet who just wants to get the best out of my dad...who won’t judge me for the things I feel or...try to change me into something else.
: I will judge you heavily for the things you feel. And I can almost guarantee I’d try to change you as well as I can not even fathom living with a creature like you.
: Just saying...you’re the closest to my real mom that my dad can get. At least...among those his age.
: And I think you guys would make a really sweet couple if you weren’t already a lesbian.
: I’m...bisexual, technically.
: Oh.
: Well, maybe there’s hope after all then?
: Hope for what? This is absolutely not how this conversation is supposed to end. I didn’t drag you here to ask for your blessing. Plus, I’m already in a relationship. Mostly.
: Just saying! I might not have ever left at all if you were the one in Niki’s place!
: So you’ll go back then? To Arakawa’s-
: Maybe! Later, Miss Watabe! This was actually a pretty productive talk!
: Wait! Ami-
: Fucking Arakawas...
: Ending every single conversation by just making me more confused...
: Ugh...
: I want to fucking die.
Ami is now PENDING!
